challenge_families.prompt: For pea pod colour, G (green) is dominant to g (yellow). Cross Gg × Gg. Show the gametes, give the genotype and phenotype proportions, and calculate the expected numbers of each phenotype among 284 offspring. If actual small-sample results differ from the expected counts, does that alone disprove Mendelian segregation? Explain.
challenge_families.answer: Gamete types: G, g and G, g. Genotypes: GG: 1/4, Gg: 2/4, gg: 1/4. Phenotypes: green: 3/4, expected 213, yellow: 1/4, expected 71. Expected counts are theoretical, not a guarantee for a small sample. No. Random fertilisation causes sampling variation; test larger, well-controlled data before drawing that conclusion.

challenge_families.prompt: Of 48 stomata examined before drought, 24 are open. After water stress, only 12 are open. Find the before/after percentage open and explain the roles of guard-cell turgor and ABA. Give one trade-off of closure. A student claims that reduced transpiration always increases growth. Evaluate the claim using CO₂ entry and cooling.
challenge_families.answer: Before=50.00%; after=25.00%. Guard-cell turgor controls the pore; ABA promotes closure during stress. Closure conserves water but restricts CO₂ uptake and can reduce photosynthesis. Not always: reduced CO₂ entry may limit photosynthesis and reduced evaporative cooling may raise leaf temperature, even though water is conserved.
challenge_families.family: Twist: benefit and trade-off of closure

challenge_families.prompt: A potato strip initially has mass 2.3 g. After immersion in 15% sucrose solution it has mass 1.0 g. Calculate percentage mass change and explain the direction of water movement through the cell membrane. Assume no tissue loss. Predict whether a boiled, membrane-damaged strip should be interpreted using the same selectively permeable-cell model.
challenge_families.answer: Mass change=-1.3 g; percentage=-56.52%. Water moves out by exosmosis into the more concentrated external solution; cells lose turgor and may plasmolyse. Not without qualification: boiling disrupts living membranes; the selective barrier assumed in the model may no longer function.

challenge_families.prompt: A plant is kept in darkness for 46 hours, then used with an opaque cover over part of a leaf and exposed to light for 8 hours. State the aim, explain destarching, predict the iodine-test result and state a relevant control/comparison. Explain why a positive iodine test in a plant that was not destarched could not by itself prove starch was made during the experiment.
challenge_families.answer: Aim: test the requirement for light. Darkness uses stored starch, so new starch can be attributed to the test conditions. The covered part lacks light and does not form starch, while exposed photosynthetic tissue turns blue-black. Previously stored starch may remain; destarching helps isolate starch formed under the experimental conditions.

challenge_families.prompt: A simplified kidney model forms 133 L filtrate per day and produces 1.3 L urine. Calculate the volume and percentage reabsorbed. Name the filtration site and explain why normal urine should not contain large plasma proteins. A student calls the entire filtrate volume “water lost from the body”. Correct this claim.
challenge_families.answer: Reabsorbed=131.7 L; percentage=99.02%. Ultrafiltration occurs at the glomerulus into Bowman’s capsule. The filtration barrier normally retains blood cells and large proteins. Most filtered water is reabsorbed to blood; only the final excreted fraction is lost as urine.

challenge_families.prompt: A diploid cell with 16 chromosomes is observed at metaphase of mitosis, before centromeres divide. State chromosome number, chromatid number, chromosome arrangement and the structure attaching spindle fibres to chromosomes. Explain how DNA can have replicated even though the chromosome number has not doubled at metaphase.
challenge_families.answer: 16 chromosomes, 32 chromatids. Chromosomes align at the equator; spindle fibres attach at the centromere/kinetochore region. Do not double chromosome number merely because each chromosome has two chromatids. DNA replication forms sister chromatids; chromosome count is based on centromeres until they separate.
challenge_families.family: Twist: DNA amount versus chromosome count

challenge_families.prompt: A town starts a year with 42000 people. There are 414 births, 389 deaths, 136 immigrants and 151 emigrants. Find population at year-end and natural increase. Explain why natural increase alone does not give the total change. Could this town have positive natural increase yet a falling total population? State the required migration condition.
challenge_families.answer: Natural increase=25. Total change=births−deaths+immigration−emigration=10; final population=42010. Migration also affects population size. Yes, if net emigration exceeds births minus deaths; total change then becomes negative.

challenge_families.prompt: A model moth population changes from 52% dark forms among 127 moths to 95% after 10 generations on darkened tree trunks. Explain natural selection using variation, differential survival and inheritance. Why is “each moth changed colour because it needed to” an incorrect explanation? If the background becomes light again, must every dark moth disappear immediately? Explain.
challenge_families.answer: Pre-existing heritable variation gives some moths better camouflage. Reduced predation increases their survival/reproduction; inherited variants become more frequent. Individuals do not intentionally acquire the needed inherited colour. Selection changes frequencies across generations. No. Selection changes reproductive success over generations; surviving frequencies, migration and other conditions matter.
challenge_families.family: Twist: selection is not immediate transformation

challenge_families.prompt: After 67 seconds of a circulation-tracing simulation, a marker is reported at right ventricle. State the next major route it follows, the oxygenation change across the relevant capillary bed, and why valves are needed. Give one artery carrying deoxygenated blood and one vein carrying oxygenated blood in the adult pulmonary circuit.
challenge_families.answer: Route: pulmonary artery → lung capillaries → pulmonary veins → left atrium. Pulmonary capillaries oxygenate blood; systemic capillaries supply tissues and collect CO₂. Valves maintain one-way flow by preventing backflow. Arteries are named by direction away from the heart, not oxygen content. Pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood away from the right ventricle; pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood to the left atrium.
challenge_families.family: Twist: artery does not mean oxygenated

challenge_families.prompt: A water plant releases 42 bubbles in 6 minutes under one light condition and 57 bubbles in the same time under brighter light. Calculate both rates, infer the effect of light and give one reason bubble count is only an approximate measure of photosynthesis. The brighter lamp also warmed the water. Explain why the result cannot isolate light intensity as the only cause.
challenge_families.answer: Rates=7.00 and 9.50 bubbles/min. The higher rate is consistent with increased photosynthesis when light was limiting. Bubble sizes vary and some oxygen dissolves; keep plant size, temperature and CO₂ supply controlled. Temperature changed as well and can affect metabolic rate; control it independently before attributing the difference solely to light.

challenge_families.prompt: 190 g limestone yields 25.536 L CO₂ at STP on complete reaction with excess HCl. Find its CaCO₃ percentage purity. A pupil divides CO₂ mass directly by sample mass to report purity. Explain the mistake. CaCO₃=100, CO₂=44 g/mol.
challenge_families.answer: n(CO₂)=25.536/22.4=1.14; same moles CaCO₃, mass=114 g. Purity=60%. CO₂ mass is not CaCO₃ mass; convert with the stoichiometric molar-mass ratio.

challenge_families.prompt: A cell contains 82 cm³ aqueous CuSO₄ and pure copper electrodes. State changes at both electrodes, write both electrode equations and explain whether the blue colour should fade substantially during ideal operation. A student says the copper cathode gains mass because negative electrons are deposited as metal. Correct the explanation.
challenge_families.answer: Anode copper dissolves: Cu→Cu²⁺+2e⁻. Cathode copper deposits: Cu²⁺+2e⁻→Cu. Copper ions used at the cathode are replenished at the anode, so blue colour remains approximately constant. Copper ions gain electrons and become neutral copper atoms; electrons alone do not supply the metal mass.
challenge_families.family: Twist: ions versus electrons at a cathode

challenge_families.prompt: A 3 V test circuit is connected to a cell containing 147 cm³ of molten NaCl. Predict whether it conducts and explain the charge carriers. Why is merely dissolving a substance insufficient to guarantee conduction? Distinguish ionisation from simple physical dissolution in your explanation.
challenge_families.answer: It conducts: its ions are mobile. Conduction requires mobile charged particles; a molecular solute can dissolve without producing ions. Ionic dissociation separates pre-existing ions; ionisation forms ions from molecules. Mere dissolution can leave neutral molecules.
challenge_families.family: Twist: dissolution does not guarantee ions

challenge_families.prompt: X has atomic number 12, mass number 28, and forms an ion with charge +2. Find protons, neutrons and electrons in the ion. Explain whether ion formation changes the nucleus. Another sample has the same atomic number and two more neutrons. Will its usual valency differ? Justify.
challenge_families.answer: p=12; n=16; electrons=Z−charge=10. Forming the ion changes electrons only, not protons or neutrons. It is an isotope with the same electron configuration (for the same charge), so its usual chemical valency is unchanged.
challenge_families.mcqPrompt: An ion has atomic number 12, mass number 28, and charge +2. How many electrons does it have?

challenge_families.prompt: Analysis of 154 g of a C/O compound gives 42 g carbon and 112 g oxygen. Its relative molecular mass is 44. Find empirical and molecular formulae. C=12, O=16. State why percentage composition alone could not have fixed the molecular formula.
challenge_families.answer: Moles C=3.5, O=7. Divide by 3.5: C:O=1:2. Empirical formula CO2, mass 44. Molecular multiplier=1; formula C1O2. The empirical ratio can be multiplied by an integer; molecular mass is needed to select the multiplier.

challenge_families.prompt: You are given 122 cm³ of a gas believed to be sulphur dioxide. State the expected confirmatory test result and explain why a change in litmus alone is insufficient to distinguish every gas. Give its formula and relative molecular mass. A dry litmus paper shows no change with dry HCl. Does that disprove the gas identity? Explain the role of moisture.
challenge_families.answer: Sulphur dioxide: acidified potassium dichromate changes from orange to green. Formula SO₂, relative molecular mass 64. Several acidic gases turn blue litmus red, so a more specific reaction/test is needed for identification. No. HCl needs water to ionise and display its acidic effect on litmus; damp paper is required.
challenge_families.family: Twist: dry gas and dry indicator

challenge_families.prompt: 89.6 g copper reacts with excess dilute nitric acid. Write the equation, identify the main nitrogen oxide, describe its appearance and calculate its amount in moles. Cu=64 g/mol. Explain why using the ordinary metal+dilute-acid rule to predict hydrogen here would fail.
challenge_families.answer: 3Cu+8HNO₃→3Cu(NO₃)₂+2NO+4H₂O. Copper moles=1.4; gas moles=0.933. NO is colourless and turns brown in air as it forms NO₂. Nitric acid is an oxidising acid; for copper the supplied concentration determines the nitrogen oxide product, rather than liberation of hydrogen.

challenge_families.prompt: A hydrocarbon is an acyclic alkyne with one triple bond and has 3 carbon atoms. Write its formula, calculate the H₂ moles needed to fully hydrogenate 6.2 mol, and name a suitable catalyst. Both the original and fully hydrogenated products are colourless gases in this description. Why is appearance not a sufficient test for unsaturation?
challenge_families.answer: Formula C3H4. Each triple bond takes 2 mol H₂ per mol, so H₂ needed=12.4 mol. Use nickel under suitable heating conditions. A specific addition reaction such as bromine decolourisation tests bonding; colourless appearance alone reveals no bond multiplicity.

challenge_families.prompt: A 2.6 cm³ sample containing Zn²⁺ ions is tested by adding NH₄OH dropwise, then in excess. Describe the observations, name/formulate the precipitate, and explain why “white precipitate” alone is not a unique identification. Explain why adding the reagent in excess must be recorded as a separate observation from its initial addition.
challenge_families.answer: Precipitate: white gelatinous precipitate; formula Zn(OH)₂. In excess: soluble in excess NH₄OH. More than one cation can form a white precipitate; excess-reagent behaviour and a second test are required. Some initially similar precipitates dissolve in excess reagent; initial colour alone can miss the distinguishing behaviour.

challenge_families.prompt: Equal volumes (14.56 L each) of nitrogen and ammonia are measured at the same STP conditions. Compare their numbers of molecules and calculate their masses. Molar masses: 28 and 17 g/mol. A classmate says equal molecules require equal total atoms. Is that necessarily true?
challenge_families.answer: By Avogadro’s law equal volumes at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules. Each contains 0.65 mol. Masses=18.2 g and 11.05 g. Equal volume does not imply equal mass. No: molecular atomicity can differ (for example two atoms in H₂ and three in CO₂), so count atoms per molecule as well.

challenge_families.prompt: A customer has exactly ₹8778. An article is marked ₹8800, and GST at 5% is payable after discount. What minimum percentage discount makes the invoice exactly equal to the money available? Show why applying the discount after GST gives the same numerical invoice here.
challenge_families.answer: Let discount=d%. 8800(1−d/100)(105/100)=8778 gives d=5%. Percentage factors multiply commutatively when both are applied to the same price chain; tax itself is calculated on the discounted value.

challenge_families.prompt: A student obtains x=8 and x=−8 while solving a rectangle problem with breadth x. The rectangle has length x+0 and area 64. Explain which root is physically admissible and find the actual dimensions. Explain why an algebraically valid root may be rejected.
challenge_families.answer: Positive root x=8 is the breadth; length=8. Root −8 makes the breadth negative and is inadmissible. Dimensions 8 by 8; area=64. The model imposes positive lengths.

challenge_families.prompt: Two similar triangles have corresponding side ratio 8:13. A student multiplies the smaller area 448 cm² by 13/8 to obtain the larger area. Correct the method, calculate the larger area, and find the scale factor for perimeters.
challenge_families.answer: Areas scale by the square of the side factor. Larger area=448×(13/8)²=1183 cm². Perimeters scale by 13:8. The student used a linear factor on an area.

challenge_families.prompt: From an external point P a tangent PA has length 10 cm. A secant through P meets the circle first at B and then C; PB=2 cm. Find PC and BC. All lengths are measured along the same secant. A student treats the supplied PB as BC. Explain the difference and identify the first point at which the secant meets the circle.
challenge_families.answer: Tangent-secant theorem: PA²=PB×PC. PC=100/2=50 cm. BC=PC−PB=48 cm. PB is the outside segment and BC lies inside the circle; B is the nearer intersection.

challenge_families.prompt: A class records 5 students scoring 16 and 9 students scoring 32. A student reports the mean as (16+32)/2. Find the correct mean and show when that shortcut would be valid.
challenge_families.answer: Weighted mean=(5×16+9×32)/14=26.29. The shortcut is valid if frequencies are equal (or if the two scores coincide). Here the frequencies differ.

challenge_families.prompt: The values [6, 12, 18] have frequencies 2, k, 2 respectively. Their mean is 12. Can k be determined uniquely? Justify your answer, assuming k is a positive integer.
challenge_families.answer: Σfx=48+12k; Σf=4+k. The mean simplifies to 12 for every positive k. The information does not determine k uniquely.

challenge_families.prompt: A(-3,0) and B(7,20) are divided internally by P in ratio AP:PB=1:4. Find P and verify the ratio using the change in x-coordinates. A student reverses the weights m and n in the formula. State which endpoint must receive the coefficient m when AP:PB=m:n.
challenge_families.answer: P=((4×-3+1×7)/5,(4×0+1×20)/5)=(-1,4). The x-distances are 2 and 8, ratio 1:4. Endpoint B receives m; endpoint A receives n.

challenge_families.prompt: A bag has 6 red, 2 blue and 7 green balls. One ball is drawn. A student adds P(not red)+P(not blue) to calculate P(red or blue). Find both quantities and explain the overcounting.
challenge_families.answer: P(red or blue)=8/15. P(not red)+P(not blue)=22/15. Green belongs to both complement events and is counted twice; the sum is not the requested union.
challenge_families.family: Twist: overlapping events on a single draw

challenge_families.prompt: ₹700 is deposited at the beginning of each month for 24 months in a recurring deposit earning 6% p.a. Use the standard ICSE RD formula to find interest and maturity. A classmate uses simple interest on nP for the whole n-month term. Explain why this overestimates the interest.
challenge_families.answer: I = Pn(n+1)r/2400. Here I = ₹1050. M = nP + I = ₹17850. For the inverse problem, P = M/[n + n(n+1)r/2400] = ₹700. Later instalments earn for fewer months; the balances do not all remain deposited for n months.
challenge_families.mcqPrompt: Find the interest on monthly RD instalments ₹700 for 24 months at 6% p.a. using I = Pn(n+1)r/2400.

challenge_families.prompt: A surveyor’s eye is 1.8 m above horizontal ground. The tower base is 62 m away and the elevation of the top is 45°. A solution gives 62tan(45°) as the tower height. Identify the missing term and calculate the height to 2 decimal places.
challenge_families.answer: The triangle gives height above the eye, not above ground. Add 1.8 m: h=62tan(45°)+1.8=63.80 m.

challenge_families.prompt: A student claims that replacing series resistors 11 Ω and 16 Ω with a parallel connection across the SAME ideal 18 V battery reduces current because “current divides”. Calculate total current in both cases and evaluate the claim.
challenge_families.answer: Series current=0.667 A. Parallel current=V(1/R1+1/R2)=2.761 A. Current divides between branches, but total current increases because equivalent resistance falls from 27 to 176/27 Ω.

challenge_families.prompt: An object is 12 cm to the left of a convex lens of focal length magnitude 15 cm. Light travels left to right. Use Cartesian signs to find image distance, magnification and image nature. A student rejects a negative image distance as impossible. Evaluate the objection.
challenge_families.answer: u=-12 cm, f=15 cm. 1/v−1/u=1/f gives v=-60.00 cm. m=v/u=5.00. Image is virtual, erect. A negative v places it on the object side. A negative v is valid: it indicates a virtual image on the object side.

challenge_families.prompt: 300 g water at 23°C is mixed with 300 g ice at 0°C in an insulated vessel. With cwater=4.2 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹ and L=336 J/g, determine whether all the ice melts, the final temperature, and the mass of ice remaining.
challenge_families.answer: Water cooling to 0°C supplies 28980 J. This melts 86.25 g, less than 300 g. Ice remains, so equilibrium temperature is 0°C. Remaining ice=213.75 g. Do not use a liquid-only average-temperature formula.

challenge_families.prompt: A heater is rated 1300 W, 230 V. Calculate its rated current and resistance. Assuming resistance is constant, find its power when operated at 115 V. Explain why doubling voltage does not merely double power under the stated assumption.
challenge_families.answer: I=P/V=5.652 A. R=V²/P=40.692 Ω. At half voltage, P′=V′²/R=P/4=325.0 W. This assumes unchanged resistance. Since P=V²/R and R is fixed, doubling voltage multiplies power by four.

challenge_families.prompt: A motor consuming electrical power raises 74 kg through 13 m in 19 s. Its efficiency is 40%. Find the minimum electrical input power. A student divides the output by 40; identify the unit error.
challenge_families.answer: Useful output=mgh/t=506.316 W. Fractional efficiency=0.4. Input=output/(40/100)=1265.789 W. Efficiency percent must be converted to a fraction before dividing.

challenge_families.prompt: A tuning fork of frequency 480 Hz sends a wave from air (speed 330 m/s) into water (speed 1320 m/s). A pupil says both pitch and wavelength become four times as large. Correct both statements and calculate both wavelengths.
challenge_families.answer: Frequency and therefore pitch remain unchanged at the boundary. λair=0.688 m; λwater=2.750 m. Wavelength alone becomes four times as large.

challenge_families.prompt: A light horizontal beam is supported at a pivot. A 90 N load is 40 cm to the left. What downward force at 10 cm to the right balances it? Find the upward reaction at the pivot. Now a downward 20 N beam weight acts exactly through the pivot. State what changes and what does not.
challenge_families.answer: Clockwise moment=anticlockwise moment: F×10=90×40. F=360 N. Vertical balance gives reaction=90+360=450 N. The beam weight is neglected. The added weight has no moment about the pivot, so the balancing force is unchanged; the upward reaction increases by 20 N.

challenge_families.prompt: A nucleus has mass number 159 and atomic number 64. It emits 3 alpha particle(s) and then 1 beta-minus particle(s). Find the final mass and atomic numbers and explain whether a following gamma emission changes either. A pupil concludes that unchanged mass number after beta emission means no change of element. Explain the mistake.
challenge_families.answer: Each α reduces A by 4 and Z by 2; each β⁻ leaves A unchanged and increases Z by 1. Final A=147; Z=59. Gamma emission changes neither A nor Z. Element identity is set by atomic number, which changes during beta-minus emission.
challenge_families.family: Twist: element identity in beta decay

challenge_families.prompt: Appliances rated [500, 1500, 100] W operate simultaneously on a 240 V supply. Find their total current. Select the smallest suitable fuse from 3 A, 5 A, 10 A, 13 A, 15 A, 20 A, 25 A, taking a rating strictly above normal current. State which wire contains it. Explain why putting the fuse in the neutral wire can leave a hazard even after it melts.
challenge_families.answer: Ptotal=2100 W; I=P/V=8.75 A. Select 10 A under the stated rule. The fuse must be in the live wire so that melting disconnects the appliance from the live supply. The appliance may remain connected to the live conductor even when the neutral path opens.

challenge_families.prompt: 50 g of water at 73°C is mixed with 350 g of water at 22°C in an insulated container of negligible heat capacity. Find the final temperature. State the heat-balance equation. Would a real vessel initially at the colder temperature make the final temperature higher or lower than your ideal result? Give a reason.
challenge_families.answer: Heat lost=heat gained: 50c(73−T)=350c(T−22). T=(50×73+350×22)/400=28.38°C. The result lies between the starting temperatures. Lower: the vessel also gains heat, so less is available to warm the colder water.
